2.17

trees <- data.frame(health=c("infected", "uninfected"))
prior <- c(.18,.82)
data <- c("maple", "other")

set.seed(84735)

trees_sim <- sample_n(trees, size=10000, weight=prior, replace=TRUE) %>%
  mutate(data_model = case_when(health=="infected" ~ .8,
                                health=="uninfected" ~ .1)) %>%
  group_by(1:n()) %>%
  mutate(species=sample(data, size=1, prob=c(data_model, 1-data_model)))
  
trees_sim %>% tabyl(species,health) %>%
  adorn_totals(c("col","row"))
 species infected uninfected Total
   maple     1482        860  2342
   other      363       7295  7658
   Total     1845       8155 10000

2.18

# Define possible values of pi
lactose <- data.frame(pi = c(0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7))

# Define the prior model
prior <- c(0.1, 0.2, 0.44, 0.26)

# Simulate 10000 values of pi from the prior
set.seed(84735)
lactose_sim <- sample_n(lactose, size = 10000, weight = prior, replace = TRUE)

# Simulate 10000 samples
lactose_sim <- lactose_sim %>% 
  mutate(y = rbinom(10000, size = 80, prob = pi))

# Focus on simulations with y = 47
filtered <- lactose_sim %>% 
  filter(y == 47)

# Summarize the posterior approximation
filtered %>% 
  tabyl(pi) %>% 
  adorn_totals("row")
    pi   n    percent
   0.5  50 0.10683761
   0.6 399 0.85256410
   0.7  19 0.04059829
 Total 468 1.00000000
# Plot the posterior approximation
ggplot(filtered, aes(x = pi, y=after_stat(count)/sum(after_stat(count)))) + 
  geom_bar()

3.16

  1. The prior distribution is centered close to 1 with little variability, so prior beliefs are very confident that the true proportion \(\pi\) is near 1. The likelihood based on the data is centered near 0.25 with almost no density greater than 0.4. So these represent very different distributions.

  2. The posterior is centered around 0.75 with nearly all its density between 0.65 and 0.85. The posterior mean is much closer to the prior mean than to the data mean.

Kimya thinks that the probability the shop is open is probably somewhat small, and that as the probability of being open increases the chance that probability is true decreases linearly. Fernando has similar thoughts but the chance of the probability being true decreases in a more exponential fashion. 4.18

  1. Beta(4,4), Beta(7,11), Beta(27,91)
#b
plot_beta(4,3)

plot_beta(4,4)

plot_beta(7,11)

plot_beta(27,91)

At first the employee was fairly uncertain about pi, although they thought it was more likely to be larger than 0.5 than smaller than 0.5. After the first day they were still fairly uncertain and also now thought that it was equally likely to be above 0.5 as below 0.5. After the second day they became convinced it was lower than 0.75 and also ruled out any values below about 0.1, with the most plausible values of pi being around 0.4. After the third day they narrowed down their understanding even more, now thinking pi must be between 0.12 and 0.35 with the most likely value slightly below 1/4.

  1. It would be a Beta(27,91), the same as the sequentially obtained posterior.
